Chronoscope: Developmental Parameter Decomposition (DPD). Use the training trajectory as the third tensor mode that makes weight-space mechanisms identifiable, then build a mechanism-by-data-by-time ledger of learning.
Nats of Understanding: turn explanations into executable code, swap them into the model, and measure in nats how much of a network we actually understand
Binding Autoencoders: unsupervised discovery of role–filler (tensor-product) structure that SAEs cannot see
Mediation-Faithful Circuit Tracing: test every attribution-graph edge against the real model, and train replacement models that pass (mediated Jacobian matching plus interventional consistency)
Occam Causal Abstraction: null-calibrated, description-length causal abstraction with a representation-format ladder
Atlas Transcoders and Variable Graphs: finding the continuous variables a network computes with, and the functions between them
GeoTrace: geometric replacement models and manifold attribution graphs
The Representation Census: typed, complete decompositions checked against known-world model organisms (settling what dark matter is, and which ontology is right)

Developmental Knockout Screen: a CRISPR-style interventional map of which mechanisms are prerequisites, scaffolds, or competitors for others during training
Error-Correction Spectroscopy: measuring superposition and feature validity from the model's own defenses
Answer-Key Language Models: training realistic small LMs with certified planted mechanisms and a superposition dial, to measure when each interpretability method sees the truth
POPPER: adversarial explainer–falsifier self-play over executable mechanistic simulators, scored by held-out intervention prediction
Geometric Circuit Tracing: attribution graphs whose nodes are manifolds and whose edges are named geometric operations
The Free-Energy Ledger: a falsifiable, quantitative law for which mechanism forms when, tested by pre-registered interventions on data frequency and mechanism complexity
WEIGHTREADER: an amortized decompiler that reads SGD-trained transformer weights and writes the program they actually run (with population-scale 'ecology of algorithms')

prior_work_found: Matena & Raffel, NPEFF: Uncovering Model Processing Strategies with Non-Negative Per-Example Fisher Factorization (v3 June 2026). CLOSEST PRIOR, and the proposal does not cite it. It decomposes per-example Fisher (gradient) attributions additively and non-negatively into components ('processing strategies'). It runs on decoder LMs (SmolLM2-360M/1.7B, GPT-2 medium). It argues that behaviors are 'polygenic' and that gradient clustering 'essentially guarantees the recovery of only monogenic factors'. It beats gradient clustering and SAEs. It validates components with targeted parameter perturbations and top-vs-random KL selectivity ratios. It explicitly leaves 'circuits corresponding to components' as future work. https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04649

Chrisman, Bushnaq & Sharkey 2025, L3D: Identifying Sparsely Active Circuits Through Local Loss Landscape Decomposition. A sparse dictionary of parameter directions reconstructs per-sample loss gradients, and it is validated by perturbations that affect only the relevant samples. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.00194

Baker, Wang, Hoogland & Murfet 2025, Structural Inference with Susceptibilities. A per-token x component response matrix whose low-rank structure separates induction and multigram modules (3M-parameter LM). https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.18274 ; Wang et al. 2025, Embryology of a Language Model (UMAP of susceptibilities gives a 'body plan', induction, and a 'spacing fin'). https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.00331

Golimblevskaia et al. 2025/2026, Circuit Insights (CircuitLens). Uses transcoder features plus attention-head contributions as a shared coordinate system and clusters inputs by circuit (Jaccard + DBSCAN) on Gemma-2-2B with GemmaScope transcoders. This is per feature, not model-wide, but it already uses the proposal's 'key insight'. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.14936
Arora, Wu, Steinhardt & Schwettmann 2026, ADAG: Automatically Describing Attribution Graphs (attribution profiles plus clustering of features into supernodes). https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07615

Patel, Zhang & Hu 2026, LLMs Can Annotate Attribution Graphs (1,000 Wikipedia attribution graphs, annotated one graph at a time with no cross-graph mechanism dictionary). https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02632
Michaud et al. 2023, Quantization Model / QDG. https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.13506 ; Marks et al. 2024, Sparse Feature Circuits. https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19647

Liu, Liu & Gore 2025 (NeurIPS 2025 best paper runner-up), Superposition Yields Robust Neural Scaling. Under strong superposition, loss scaling is robust to the feature-frequency distribution, which confounds the proposal's frequency-exponent test of the quantization model. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10465
Bayat Makou et al. 2026, Many Circuits, One Mechanism (phantom specialization: structurally distinct circuits implement the same computation). https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06267

Parameter decomposition has moved past toy models: Decomposition of Small Transformer Models (SPD on GPT-2 small) https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08854 ; Targeted PD on 4- and 12-block Pile LMs https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13047 ; ASPD on Qwen-3-8B, which composes read/write weight components into mechanism circuits https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37731

Within-graph or cross-circuit aggregation, none of which learns a corpus-level mechanism dictionary: HAGD https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12879 ; Aljaafari et al. ILP circuit signatures https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21303 ; Circuit-Diff https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23892 ; concept-targeted attribution https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27510 ; Wang, Communication Map (weights-only) https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22007 ; circuit-motifs repo (motif census over 99 graphs, no dictionary) https://github.com/mkenney2/circuit-motifs

Vision precedents for clustering per-sample attributions into global strategies: SpRAy (Lapuschkin et al. 2019) https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10178 ; PCX prototypical concept explanations (Dreyer et al. 2023) https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.16681

The open problem is confirmed only as a proposal, with no implemented results: Circuits Research Landscape, Aug 2025 ('Can we merge attribution graphs, or otherwise obtain a more global circuit picture?') https://www.neuronpedia.org/graph/info

Feasibility check: Gemma Scope 2 ships PT and IT dictionaries for 270M/1B/4B/12B/27B, including transcoder_all (every layer) and CLTs, with small/medium/large L0 variants. https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-scope-2-270m-pt
verdicts.fatal_issues:
I found no published method that learns a sparse dictionary over per-token attribution-graph edge-influence vectors to build a corpus-level, loss-covering mechanism catalog. So the specific method looks novel and survives. Several of the proposal's headline claims are overstated or invalid as written, though. Unfixed, they would sink it in review.

(1) The novelty framing is wrong.
- NPEFF (2310.04649, revised June 2026, on decoder LMs) already does additive, non-negative, polygenic decomposition of per-example attributions into strategies.
- NPEFF already makes the 'clustering only recovers monogenic factors' argument, almost word for word.
- NPEFF already beats gradient clustering and SAEs.
- NPEFF already validates components with selective perturbations, using top-vs-random selectivity ratios.
- L3D does the same for sparse per-sample gradient subnetworks, and susceptibility matrices do it for per-token x component modules.
- CircuitLens already uses transcoder features as a shared cross-input coordinate system to cluster inputs by circuit.
So 'the key insight', 'unlike clustering, mechanisms can co-occur', 'monogenic vs polygenic' and 'analogue of the SAE step-change for computation' are not new. What is new is narrower: the atoms are readable feature-level subgraphs (NPEFF explicitly leaves that to future work), measured over the LM pretraining distribution, with loss coverage and cross-model / PT-vs-IT comparisons. The baselines also omit NPEFF and L3D, which are the true competitors.

(2) The quantization-model test is not falsifiable as specified.
- Heavy-tailed atom frequencies are nearly guaranteed by Zipfian token statistics.
- Dictionary-learning artifacts push the same way: atoms split as K grows, and NPEFF reports the same splitting.
- Liu, Liu & Gore (2505.10465) show that power-law loss scaling arises under strong superposition regardless of the frequency distribution, so matching or mismatching exponents does not discriminate between theories.
- 'Not heavy-tailed means the quantization model fails' is not a real falsification.

(3) Phantom specialization (2606.06267) undermines the census. Edge-keyed atoms will split one functional mechanism into many structurally distinct atoms. Atom counts also depend on transcoder width, L0 and feature absorption, so 'how many mechanisms a model has' is ill-defined without functional-equivalence merging.

(4) The compute estimate is likely about 10x optimistic.
- Full-sequence adjacency needs roughly one backward pass per active node, batched in circuit-tracer style. That is about 1e4 to 1e5 nodes per 64-128-token sequence.
- At that size, 0.5-2 s per sequence for Gemma 3 270M is unrealistic.
- 'Overnight on CPU' for 20k GPT-2 positions is optimistic: my rough estimate is 1-2 days without aggressive pruning.

(5) Attribution graphs freeze attention patterns. QK-implemented mechanisms, such as induction matching, are therefore invisible to the OV/MLP edge vocabulary, which biases the census toward MLP and OV mechanisms.

Coverage caveat: the WebSearch budget ran out early. The rest of the search used the arXiv listing and abstract pages, GitHub search and direct page fetches. LessWrong/AF search pages render client-side and returned nothing, so there may be informal AF/LW work I could not check.
verdicts.fixes:
1. Reposition the contribution and add the right baselines.
- Frame it as 'polygenic mechanism decomposition (NPEFF/L3D lineage) moved into attribution-graph edge space, so every atom is a readable, causally checkable feature-level circuit'. This is the step NPEFF leaves as future work.
- Cite NPEFF, L3D, susceptibilities, CircuitLens, ADAG, SpRAy and PCX.
- Make NPEFF the primary baseline, with L3D if tractable and an SVD/NMF of a susceptibility-style token x component matrix. QDG and k-means stay as secondary baselines.
- At equal K, compare on four things: selectivity ratio, loss coverage, interpretability, and cross-method agreement (do edge atoms align with NPEFF components on the same tokens?).

2. Add a ground-truth tier before any LM claims.
- Train small transformers on a Zipf-weighted mixture of planted mechanisms, e.g. Michaud's multitask sparse parity plus induction, bigram, bracket-matching and modular-addition subtasks that co-occur within sequences.
- Train transcoders on them and show that atoms recover the planted mechanisms, including co-active ones, while QDG and NPEFF do or do not.
- This tier is the decisive, cheap, falsifiable demo, and it calibrates the census.

3. Make the census well-defined.
- Merge atoms that are functionally equivalent. Two atoms count as one mechanism if they are causally interchangeable (interchange intervention or mutual ablation transfer), following 2606.06267.
- Report counts as curves over dictionary K, transcoder width (16k/64k/256k) and L0 (small/medium/large in Gemma Scope 2), choosing K by MDL or held-out coverage.
- Lead with the coverage curve, not an absolute count.

4. Redesign the quantization-model test so it can actually fail.
- Use the Pythia suite (70M-1.4B, shared tokenizer, training checkpoints) or Gemma 3 270M/1B/4B. Match atoms across sizes and steps.
- Test the distinctive prediction: atoms are acquired in order of their frequency, and the loss reduction between sizes is concentrated on tokens whose atoms are newly acquired. The rival prediction is smooth improvement across all atoms, which the superposition account of 2505.10465 predicts.
- Include frequency nulls: token unigram/bigram Zipf, transcoder feature frequencies, atoms from random-init or shuffled models, and exponent stability across K and L0.
- Drop 'not heavy-tailed falsifies the quantization model'.

5. Make extraction feasible.
- Use two-stage pruning. First, get per-target node influence with one VJP per target position, using a linearized replacement with frozen attention and LayerNorm and stop-gradients. Then build edges only among the top-N nodes per target.
- Use 32-64-token contexts, subsample target positions, and use small-L0 transcoder_all dictionaries.
- Re-estimate costs empirically on 10 sequences before committing to the GPU tier.

6. Handle attention.
- Add Kamath et al.-style QK attribution edges as a separate relation type, or measure and report the share of loss attribution that lives in attention-pattern changes and error nodes.
- Report these as the census's 'dark matter'.

7. Keep the pre-registered criteria, but add NPEFF-matched selectivity and the ground-truth recovery score as primary endpoints.
- Make the PT-vs-IT and 270M-vs-1B mechanism diffs secondary, exploratory readouts.

prior_work_found: Chrisman, Bushnaq, Sharkey 2025, Local Loss Landscape Decomposition (L3D), https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.00194. This is the closest recipe and the proposal does not cite it. It learns low-rank parameter-space subnetworks such that a sparse subset reconstructs each sample's loss gradient. It tests specificity by perturbing a subnetwork and checking that the effect falls on the relevant samples, and it was applied to a real transformer and a CNN. It works in parameter space, not transcoder-edge space, so it is not equivalent. It does contradict the claim that parameter-space mechanism decompositions are toy-only.

Anthropic, Sparse mixtures of linear transforms (MOLT), July 2025, https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/bulk-update/index.html. Each token's MLP computation is a sparse mixture of low-rank transforms, described as 'purely computational objects'. This is a per-layer, per-token sparse dictionary of computation, and it weakens the claim to be the first 'SAE for computation'.
Farnik et al. 2025, Jacobian Sparse Autoencoders, https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18147. Sparsifies the computation (the Jacobian) between input and output latents.

Arora, Wu, Steinhardt, Schwettmann 2026, ADAG: Automatically Describing Attribution Graphs, https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07615. Defines 'attribution profiles' (input and output gradient effects) and clusters features by them. Uncited; directly relevant to grouping edges by functional role.

Automated Attribution Graph Interpretation via Probe Prompting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07002. Groups features into cross-prompt supernodes on Gemma-2-2B and validates them with about 45.6k interventions. Uncited.

Friedman and Song 2026, Circuit-Diff, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23892. Exists as cited and releases a multi-prompt aggregation tool and a supernode labeling tool. The abstract reports no evaluation of either tool.

Dunefsky et al. 2024, Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11944. Splits transcoder circuits into input-invariant and input-dependent terms, an early global-weights view.
Chen, Li, Peng 2026, Concept circuits of ViTs, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09055. Global input-invariant circuits read from CLT weights, not aggregated from instance graphs.

Minniti, Kulanthaivelu, Sproat 2026, Neural Dynamics as the Composition of Quantized Units, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32487. Recovers quanta from a checkpoint trajectory on a toy numeral-naming transformer. Relevant to the quantization-model test.

Michaud et al. 2023, Quantization Model / QDG, https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.13506, and Marks et al., Sparse Feature Circuits, https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19647. Correctly characterised by the proposal as token-clustering approaches.

Verified as real and matching the proposal's descriptions: HAGD https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12879; ILP circuit signatures https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21303; concept-targeted attribution https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27510; Many Circuits, One Mechanism https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06267 (TMLR 2026; Pythia 70M-1.4B); Communication Map https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22007 (weights only). The Neuronpedia Circuits Research Landscape does list 'Can we merge attribution graphs, or otherwise obtain a more global circuit picture?' as open (https://www.neuronpedia.org/graph/info).

Gemma Scope 2 (https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-scope-2-270m-pt) ships transcoder_all (every layer), clt, crosscoders and SAEs for Gemma 3 270M, 1B, 4B, 12B and 27B, in PT and IT, at widths 16k-1M and L0 small (10-20), medium (30-60) or large (60-150). The GPU-tier resources therefore exist. The PT and IT transcoders are trained separately.

Search limitation: the shared WebSearch budget ran out after 3 queries. The rest of the search used arXiv's own search, direct paper fetches and a GitHub repo search (one hit: peppinob-ol/attribution-graph-probing, per-prompt only). LessWrong and Alignment Forum search pages are JS-rendered and could not be checked. I found no published method that does sparse dictionary learning over per-token edge-influence vectors in transcoder coordinates, but I cannot rule out an AF/LW post.
verdicts.fatal_issues:
I found no published equivalent, so the method stands on novelty. The validity design is the problem: as written, the demo would very likely pass its pre-registered criteria without showing that atoms are mechanisms or testing the quantization model.

(1) Edge vectors are largely determined by node-level quantities. Under the frozen linearization, edge influence on token t is roughly a_i(t) * W_ij * g_j(t), where a_i is the source activation and g_j is the target node's influence on the loss at t. For same-position edges W_ij is a fixed virtual weight. For attention edges it depends on frozen attention patterns, but positions are collapsed. So e_t is close to (activation outer-product influence) masked by global weights, and a dictionary over edges is close to a dictionary over attribution-weighted feature co-activation, plus wiring that is already in the weights. The proposed falsifier, NMF on unweighted feature co-occurrence, is a straw baseline. The real null is a node-attribution dictionary (activation x influence vectors, in the style of Sparse Feature Circuits), with each atom's subgraph induced through virtual weights. Unless the method beats that null, 'computation, not representation' is not shown.

(2) Criterion 2 is close to trivially satisfied. An atom's edges exist only where its source and target features are active, so ablating it on 'inactive' tokens does almost nothing for any edge set, random partitions included, and a specificity ratio of 5x or more is guaranteed. A Spearman of 0.6 or more between predicted and actual loss change is driven by atom attribution mass and by how linear the model is locally. Feature-edge 'path patching' must also run inside the local replacement (frozen attention, LayerNorm and error terms), so the validation is partly circular. Equal-mass random edge sets would pass as well.

(3) The quantization-model test is effectively unfalsifiable as specified:
- Sparse dictionaries trained on Zipfian text almost always give heavy-tailed atom usage.
- Feature-keyed edges inherit Zipf frequencies from tokens and features.
- The frequency exponent the quantization model implies from LM parameter scaling (alpha_N about 0.07-0.08, so alpha+1 about 1.08) cannot be distinguished from Zipf's roughly 1 within realistic confidence intervals.
- The exponent and the 'number of mechanisms' also depend on K, the dictionary L0 and transcoder width (feature splitting), so 'how many mechanisms' is ill-posed.

(4) Content versus algorithm. Keying edges by specific features fragments content-general mechanisms (induction, copying, successor, two-hop lookup) into many content-specific atoms. Atoms may reduce to clusters of current token plus context topic. QK routing is frozen and invisible, so the attention-selection half of most known circuits is missing from the 'census'.

(5) The loss target is biased. The loss gradient vanishes on confidently predicted tokens, which under-weights mastered mechanisms. 'Fraction of loss explained' has no defined baseline. With top-500 edge truncation and a large error-node share (especially for the GPT-2 Dunefsky transcoders), '70% of edge mass' may be a small fraction of the model's actual loss-relevant computation.

(6) The cross-model and PT-vs-IT comparisons use separately trained transcoders, both 270M vs 1B and PT vs IT in Gemma Scope 2. Without a same-model noise floor, 'fraction matched' and 'atoms gained or lost' mostly measure how well two transcoders agree.

(7) Held-out coverage may fail because of the edge-vocabulary long tail (rare feature pairs never seen in training), not because mechanisms are absent.

(8) The 'first' claims ignore L3D, MOLT, JSAE and ADAG.
verdicts.fixes:
Required changes, with (1), (2) and (4) as the decisive ones:

(1) Pre-register the decisive null and make it primary. At equal K and atom L0, compare against:
- a node-attribution dictionary (SAE or NMF on per-token activation x influence vectors), with each atom's subgraph induced through virtual weights;
- a weight-shuffled null, where W_ij is permuted within layer pairs before edge vectors are built.
Report the fraction of edge-vector variance predictable from node quantities. The method passes only if edge atoms beat node atoms on held-out reconstruction and on the causal metrics in (2).

(2) Replace the trivial causal criteria.
- Shared-edge specificity: measure the effect on tokens where the atom's edges are present but its coefficient is low, because other atoms claim those edges. This tests whether the decomposition carves boundaries between mechanisms, not just edge presence.
- Sufficiency: keeping only a token's active atoms, with error terms frozen, should recover at least X% of loss reduction relative to a bigram baseline.
- Compare everything against equal-attribution-mass random edge sets and equal-mass node ablations.
- Run interventions in the actual model with attention recomputed and nonlinearities live, and report the gap between the frozen and unfrozen results. The linearized prediction is a secondary metric only.

(3) Add ground truth and known-mechanism recovery.
- Train a small transformer on a mixture of synthetic tasks with planted Zipfian task frequencies (in the style of Michaud's multitask sparse parity, plus induction, copying, modular arithmetic), train transcoders, and show that the atoms recover the planted tasks and the planted exponent while the node-dictionary and QDG baselines do not.
- On GPT-2 small, pre-register recovery of induction, IOI name-mover, greater-than, successor and bracket-matching atoms, each spanning many token identities, with mutual information between atom assignment and token identity below a stated threshold.

(4) Make mechanisms content-general. Add a second edge vocabulary keyed by feature families or roles (ADAG attribution-profile clusters, or Matryoshka or hierarchical groupings) and by relational attention attributes (head, relative offset). Compare the atom count and coverage of the two vocabularies; that comparison is itself the content-versus-algorithm finding. Add QK attribution (Kamath et al. 2025) for attention-mediated edges in the GPU tier.

(5) Rebuild the quantization-model test.
- Compare the atom frequency exponent against nulls (token unigram, transcoder-feature frequency, node-dictionary atom frequency) and across K, dictionary L0 and transcoder width.
- Test the model's real prediction rather than an exponent match. Across Pythia 70m-1.4b (shared tokenizer and data order) and its training checkpoints, check whether atoms are acquired in order of frequency, whether the atoms larger models add are the low-frequency ones, and whether per-atom loss reductions sum to the loss-scaling curve.

(6) Fix the target and the accounting. Use the correct-logit margin, or per-token normalized gradients as QDG does, instead of the raw loss gradient. Define 'loss explained' relative to a unigram or bigram baseline. Report error-node share, truncated mass and out-of-vocabulary edge mass separately. Restrict the edge vocabulary to edges seen at least N times.

(7) Set noise floors for comparisons. Run the census twice on the same model with different transcoders (Gemma Scope 2 16k vs 64k, small vs medium L0) to get the ceiling for cross-model matching. For PT vs IT, also run with the PT transcoder applied to the IT model, so the coordinates stay fixed.

(8) Reposition the claims. Cite L3D, MOLT, JSAE, ADAG, probe prompting and Circuit-Diff. Frame the method as an L3D-style sparse decomposition in transcoder-edge coordinates whose atoms can be read as subgraphs and aligned across models. Include a head-to-head against L3D on TinyStories-33M or GPT-2 small. Drop 'first mechanistic test of the quantization model' unless the Pythia acquisition-order test is run.

(9) Budget compute honestly. A full sequence graph needs roughly one backward pass per active node (about 35k nodes per 128-token sequence for Gemma 3 270M at small L0). Treat the CPU tier as TinyStories-33M or a synthetic-task toy with self-trained transcoders, and leave GPT-2 small as a stretch goal.

redteam.title: DECOMPILE: bits-scored, weight-free decompilation of an entire language model into a runnable, readable program (the 'explained-bits curve')

prior_work_found: Search caveat: the shared WebSearch budget ran out after about 4 queries. Prior-work search then relied on direct reads of the cited papers' related-work sections, Semantic Scholar citing-paper lists (for MIPS 2402.05110, Hayes 2606.19317, Huang 2602.08857 and Friedman 2306.01128), and the research indexes of transformer-circuits.pub and Goodfire. The Nguyen 2407.12034 and Compact Proofs citation lists could not be pulled (HTTP 429). No arXiv, GitHub or LessWrong keyword search was run. Coverage of the most recent work is therefore incomplete.

Hayes, Li, Andreas 2026, Explaining Attention with Program Synthesis, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19317. Verified: about $150 of Claude-Sonnet-4 synthesis, one program per head; mean IoU 69% (GPT-2), 74% (TinyLlama-1.1B), 79% (Llama-3B); replacing 25% of heads raises perplexity by about 16%. Heads only, with no MLP or whole-model replacement. The authors name a 'complete symbolic characterization of a LM' as future work, so a scoop is likely from this group.

Somani 2026, Towards Verifiable Transformers: Solver-Checkable Circuit Explanations, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24033. Closest pipeline overlap: removes LayerNorm from a GPT-2-scale sparsemax/LeakyReLU model, replaces retained heads with restricted-DSL programs, calibrates readouts, and solver-verifies a 3-edge quote circuit. Circuit-local only, with no whole-model or bits accounting.

Huang, Bakalova, Bhattamishra, Merrill, Hahn 2026, Discovering Interpretable Algorithms by Decompiling Transformers to RASP, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08857. Algorithmic and formal-language tasks only. Their stated view is narrower than the proposal says: it is 'unlikely that language models as a whole would be expressible as simple RASP programs', but sub-programs such as induction heads are left open.
Zhang et al. 2026, Weights to Code: Extracting Interpretable Algorithms from the Discrete Transformer, https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05770. Interpretable-by-design architecture, algorithmic tasks only.
Thurnherr & Riesen 2024, Neural Decompiling of Tracr Transformers, https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.00061. Compiled Tracr models only.

Friedman, Wettig, Chen 2023, Learning Transformer Programs, https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01128. Models trained to be decompilable by design, including NER and text-classification NLP tasks, converted to Python. Not post-hoc decompilation of an ordinary LM.

Weiss, Goldberg, Yahav 2019, Learning Deterministic Weighted Automata with Queries and Counterexamples, https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.13895. Extracts PDFAs that match the next-symbol distributions of RNN language models: a weight-free, distribution-matching surrogate of an LM, uncited by the proposal. No readability or MDL scoring, and not transformers.

Nguyen 2024, Understanding Transformers via N-gram Statistics, https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12034. N-gram rulesets built from training data match the top-1 prediction for 79% of TinyStories tokens and 68% of Wikipedia tokens. A weight-free but data-derived and uncompressed approximation. The proposal already uses it as a baseline.

Gauderis, Dooms, Homer, Ayonrinde, Wiggins 2026, From Mechanistic to Compositional Interpretability, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08934. Verified to be theory only: an MDL faithfulness-versus-complexity constrained optimisation and 'compressive refinement', described as a 'blueprint for automating'. The only computation is a hand-worked bit count for a toy linear classifier. The proposal would be the first empirical instantiation, and this group could also scoop it.
Ayonrinde, Pearce, Sharkey 2024, MDL-SAEs (Interpretability as Compression), https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11179. MDL scoring of activation explanations, evaluated on MNIST.
Gross et al. 2024, Compact Proofs, https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11779. A frontier of proof length against bound tightness on toy Max-of-K. The direct conceptual ancestor of the 'explained-bits curve'.

Bushnaq et al. 2026, VPD / Interpreting Language Model Parameters (Goodfire), https://www.goodfire.com/research/interpreting-lm-parameters. Verified: 4-layer, 67M-parameter model; 9,972 of 38,912 subcomponents alive; rounded masks recover 11.8% of compute; the decomposition is 'clearly not at all robust' to adversarial masks at 160 steps or more. Neural, with no conversion to programs.

Turner, Wu, Batson 2026, Characterizing interference weights in a tiny LM, https://transformer-circuits.pub/2026/interference_effectiveness_helpfulness/index.html. Verified: 1-layer, about 2.9M parameters, vocabulary 4096, d=256; about 331M virtual weights; 'more helpful weights than parameters'. No bits accounting.

ARC AlgZoo 2026, https://www.alignment.org/blog/algzoo-uninterpreted-models-with-fewer-than-1-500-parameters/. Verified: full surprise-accounting understanding only up to about 32 parameters; the 432-parameter model remains unexplained.

verdicts.fatal_issues:
I found no substantially equivalent published method. Nothing I found rewrites a whole natural-language transformer as a weight-free program scored in bits against its KL to the model. Novelty is plausible but carries a high scoop risk, because Hayes et al. and Gauderis et al. both name this as their next step.

The issues below are not fatal to novelty, but each would undermine the claimed result if left unfixed.

(1) Accounting loophole that would invalidate the 'bits' claim. Class predicates defined by 'a semantic category named by an LLM' or by a POS tagger bring in an external neural model whose bits are never charged. A 'weight-free' program that calls a tagger or LLM at runtime is not weight-free, and L(P) is then meaningless.

(2) 'Weight-free' is trivially achievable. Any table can be written out as Python literals, and the level-0 lift is already weight-free in this sense. The real content is readability, and nothing in the objective rewards it. Pure MDL will tend to choose neural-style compression (low-rank, quantized tables) over readable rules. With no matched-bits neural-compression baseline (quantization, pruning, low-rank, or a distilled small net at equal L), a good S(P) cannot be read as understanding rather than compression.

(3) The objective is mis-specified as a single score. N in S = L(P) + N·KL sets the trade-off arbitrarily. Rough arithmetic for the target 1-layer model: L(M) at 4 bits is about 11.6 Mbit. With N = 1M, N·KL(M‖unigram) is only a few Mbit, so even a unigram program can beat L(M) on S. The phrase 'compress until no neural weights remain' also conflicts with 'accept only if S decreases'. Only the full Pareto frontier is meaningful.

(4) The success thresholds are probably unattainable as stated. Embedding and unembedding make up roughly 70% of the parameters. EF ≥ 0.85 with L(P) ≤ 10% of L(M), about 1.2 Mbit or roughly 280 bits per vocabulary item, is very unlikely. EF normalized to unigram also flatters the result, because the direct-path bigram alone captures a large share.

(5) The induction-bump developmental criterion is impossible for 1-layer models, which cannot form induction heads. It must be stated for the 2-layer model.

(6) 'Drori-2026' could not be verified, and the paraphrase of Huang et al. overstates their conjecture.
verdicts.fixes:
Each fix below answers one of the issues above.

(a) Define L(P) as a conditional description length, L(P|B). B is a frozen, versioned, public background library: a lexicon with POS tags, WordNet categories, frequency ranks, a regex and string-ops DSL. Its size is disclosed and it is held fixed across every model and checkpoint. LLMs may propose code and names offline only. No neural model may be called at runtime inside P. Report both L(P|B) and L(B).

(b) Report the frontier, not a single score. Plot KL against bits as two curves: bits spent on named-DSL rules ('explained') and bits spent on residual tables ('dark matter', charged at full cost). Make the headline a dominance test against three matched-bits baselines:
- data-derived n-gram rulesets (Nguyen) and PDFA extraction (Weiss et al. 2019);
- heads-only and pruning-only programs;
- a neural-compression frontier of M itself (quantization plus pruning plus low-rank, and a small distilled student). The gap between this frontier and the symbolic one is a new, measurable quantity: the 'readability tax' in bits.

(c) Make the lift exact by construction for the main demo. Train the 1-layer and 2-layer models LN-free (or with frozen LN scales). Use bilinear or gated-linear MLPs, which admit exact tensor and path expansion, so no transcoder residual is needed. Run standard GELU+LN models as a secondary condition to measure the cost of nonlinearity. For MLP lifting, reuse transcoders from interp-lab.

(d) Measure KL to the model correctly. Compute sequence-level KL(M‖P) on M's own samples as well as on held-out data. Add an adversarial search for high-KL prompts, since VPD failed exactly there, and report tail quantiles by token-frequency band.

(e) Normalize EF against the bigram/direct-path program, not unigram. Replace the 10%-of-L(M) target with pre-registered frontier dominance plus error agreement above the matched-bits n-gram and PDFA baselines.

(f) Operationalize Gao's simulation metric directly. Blind human or LLM readers are given only a module's docstring and DSL source and must predict its outputs on a random sample. The share of KL reduction carried by modules that pass this test is the 'understood fraction'. If it is nonzero, it is the first nonzero score on Gao's strongest metric for an LM.

(g) State the induction-bump commit test on the 2-layer model and the attention-only 2-layer model. Use the synthetic-generator language as the ground-truth calibration, and recover at least 4 of its 5 rules before any TinyStories claim.

(h) Fix the citations: add Weiss et al. 2019, Somani 2026, Friedman et al. 2023, Gross et al. 2024 (as the frontier precedent), MDL-SAEs and causal scrubbing. Drop or properly cite Drori-2026. Rephrase the Huang et al. conjecture accurately.

(i) Position the contribution as the first empirical, whole-model instantiation of MDL/compositional interpretability (Gauderis 2026) on a natural-language LM. It extends Hayes et al. from heads to the full model and Somani from circuit-local to global. Release quickly, given the scoop risk from both groups.
