verdicts.fatal_issues:
No substantially equivalent method turned up, but my search was limited. The pieces exist: path expansion (Elhage), virtual weights plus interference pruning (Turner et al. 2026), head program synthesis (Hayes et al. 2026), RASP decompilation (Huang et al. 2026) and MDL theory (Gauderis 2026, APD). No one has combined them into end-to-end, bits-priced, whole-model decompilation of a natural-language LM. The problem is that the demo as designed would not show what it claims. Its headline criteria can be met by uninformative compression, and its negative result is logically invalid.

1. Trivial-baseline inflation of EF. EF is measured as 1 − KL(M‖P)/KL(M‖unigram), and a unigram is a very weak reference. On TinyStories with a 4096-token BPE, a bigram/skip-trigram table plus within-word BPE-continuation lookups will cover most of KL(M‖unigram). EF ≥ 0.85 still allows roughly 0.3–0.5 nats of KL, which is large. EF ≥ 0.85 is therefore mostly a test of n-gram statistics, not of mechanism.

2. 'Weight-free' is just a renaming. The level-0 program is the weights written out as Python tables. The objective S(P) = L(P) + N·KL rewards compression, not readability. A low-rank or quantized table counts as 'explained' exactly like a readable rule. Neither EF nor S separates bits held in rules from bits held in tables, so 'zero model tensors' is a cosmetic milestone.

3. Free oracles leak into L(P). Class membership is free when a POS tag, a suffix regex or an 'LLM-named semantic category' defines it. That gives P a POS tagger (a spaCy model is larger than L(M)) and an LLM as unpriced oracles. 'L(P) ≤ 10% of L(M)' then becomes meaningless: the reference machine is not fixed, so the bit count can be gamed without limit.

4. The falsification clause is invalid. MDL search is incomplete (Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable). If a greedy/beam search plateaus at EF < 0.5, that bounds this search, not 'how programmable LMs are'. Without measuring the search's recall on planted programs, a negative result says nothing, and the proposal is set up so that every outcome counts as a win.

5. The error-agreement baseline is confounded. P is fit to M, while the Nguyen n-gram baseline is fit to data, and Nguyen's selection is a post-hoc oracle that cannot run on its own. Any distillation of M inherits M's errors. 'Agrees with M's mistakes more than a data n-gram does' therefore separates fit-to-M from fit-to-data, not mechanism from imitation.

6. The alignment certificate is nearly vacuous at component granularity. In an LN-free 1-layer model, logit contributions are close to additive per component. Any module that reproduces a component's output on-distribution passes the interchange test automatically. That does not rule out a module that reaches the same output through a different internal route (the 'does it its own way' failure the proposal cites as Drori 2026).

7. The calibration test is circular, and the LLM proposer can cheat. 'Recover ≥ 4/5 rules the model learned' has no independent ground truth for which rules M learned. An LLM proposer that sees text could also infer the generator from the data alone, so recovering its rules does not validate white-box decompilation.

8. The developmental criterion is weak. 'At least one program commit coincides with the induction bump' is likely to happen by chance among about 50 checkpoints with many commits, and 1-layer models do not form induction heads.

9. The targets conflict with evidence on the identical architecture. Turner et al. find helpful virtual weights outnumber the parameters of a 2.9M-parameter, d=256, 4096-vocab 1-layer model. ARC cannot fully explain a 432-parameter model. A genuine symbolic L(P) ≤ 10% of L(M) at EF 0.85 is therefore implausible, while the same thresholds are reachable by compressed tables (point 1). The criteria are too hard for real programs and too easy for tables.

10. Smaller problems:
- The choice of N in S(P) is arbitrary and decides the 'optimum'.
- LN-removal fine-tuning changes M.
- The budget does not add up: 10^4–10^5 rewrites at seconds to minutes each comes to roughly 1–70+ days, not 20–60 GPU-hours.
- Some citations overstate their sources: the D-RASP conjecture and the VPD 12% figure. The gap claim also ignores black-box weighted-automaton extraction from LMs (Eyraud & Ayache 2020).
verdicts.fixes:
Present it as 'white-box, mechanism-aligned decompilation beats black-box distillation at equal bits', and make that the falsifiable claim.

(A) Fix the reference machine.
- Define a closed DSL with a priced primitive library: tokenizer string ops and fixed token-ID sets coded at log2 C(V,k) bits.
- Charge every predicate by its exception list against its definition.
- External taggers and LLM categories are either charged at their full size or used only as documentation names, never as definitions.
- Charge fitted constants at their quantized precision.

(B) Split the ledger and the curve.
- Report L_rules (modules ≤ about 256 bits with no free tables) separately from L_tables.
- Define symbolic EF = the KL reduction achievable when tables are restricted to an M-agnostic n-gram prior.
- Plot KL against L_tables while rules stay within their per-module cap. That is the real explained-bits curve.
- Normalize EF against a matched-bits black-box distillation of M, not against a unigram: a backoff n-gram fit to M's distributions, a spectral weighted automaton in the style of Eyraud & Ayache, and a tiny student transformer at equal bits.
- Report results excluding within-word BPE continuations and by frequency band.

(C) Replace the error-agreement test with tests that black-box distillations cannot pass.
1. Ablation prediction. For each module, the paired edit in M (ablate the head, zero the subspace found by DAS, or remove a virtual-weight set) must shift M's logits the way deleting the module shifts P's. Report the correlation over all modules.
2. Off-distribution counterfactuals. Generate inputs from P's own predicates where data-fit rules and mechanism-fit rules diverge: nonsense-token contexts, swapped class members, positions outside the training length. Require KL(M‖P) there to stay close to the on-distribution value, while the black-box baselines degrade.
3. Variable-level alignment. Align each module's internal variables, such as the selector's chosen position or the class variable, to M's internal attention argmax or a DAS subspace, and measure interchange-intervention accuracy (IIA). Component-level output matching alone is not enough.

(D) Calibrate search power so negative results mean something.
- Build a planted-program suite: Tracr-compiled models, and transformers trained to imitate known stochastic programs with known S(P*).
- Include behaviorally identical twin models with different implementations, for example position-based versus content-based copying that agree on-distribution. The decompiler must tell them apart, which a black-box or LLM-reads-the-data approach cannot.
- Report recall as (bits recovered)/S(P*) and only claim bounds relative to it. Rewrite the falsification clause as 'achieved frontier given measured search recall', not 'upper bound on programmability'.
- For the synthetic language, pre-register a behavioral probe set per rule to establish which rules M actually learned, independently of the decompiler.

(E) Fix N, report the full frontier, and anchor the scale. Set N to the training token count (bits of optimization, the ARC framing) or use a prequential code. Report the whole frontier rather than one 'optimal' S.

(F) Start on the Turner et al. setting. Use the same 1L, d=256, 4096-vocab configuration, which allows direct comparison with their virtual-weight/pruning numbers. Begin with attention-only 1-layer models, where full decompilation is plausible. Present MLP 'irreducible tables' as the key quantity, priced against the black-box baselines.

(G) Developmental extension.
- Use a 2-layer model, so induction heads can form.
- Use at least 100 checkpoints, densely spaced around the phase change.
- Pre-register a test of program-diff timestamps against loss/LLC change points, with a permutation null.

(H) Budget, and two smaller fixes.
- Rewrites: 10^3–10^4 scored rewrites on cached additive 1-layer decompositions, with an early-reject screen on a 64k-token subset before any full 1M-token evaluation.
- LN: report KL(M_orig‖M_LNfree), and score P against both models.
- Citations: drop the unverified ones (the D-RASP conjecture, Drori 2026, VPD 12%).

redteam.title: Chronoscope: Developmental Parameter Decomposition (DPD). Use the training trajectory as the third tensor mode that makes weight-space mechanisms identifiable, then build a mechanism-by-data-by-time ledger of learning.

prior_work_found: CLOSEST PRIOR, Stage 1. Pellegrino, Cayco-Gajic & Chadwick, 'Low Tensor Rank Learning of Neural Dynamics', NeurIPS 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.11567. They stack weight matrices over learning into a 3-tensor and fit a CP model, W^(k) = sum_r c_r^(k) (a_r ⊗ b_r), with a smoothness prior on the trial/time factors. They discuss Kruskal-type uniqueness, validate on a GD/Adam-trained RNN (its updates were rank 2 under PARAFAC), and bound the tensor rank of gradient-descent updates. This is the same core math as DPD Stage 1, including the 'time mode gives identifiability' argument. It differs in being neuroscience RNNs in a low-rank (R of about 2 to 10), non-sparse, non-overcomplete regime, with no causal-importance refinement, no data ledger, and no transformers. The proposal does not cite it. OpenAlex shows only about 3 citing works, none in ML interpretability.

Goodfire VPD, 'Interpreting Language Model Parameters' (May 2026), https://www.goodfire.com/research/interpreting-lm-parameters. Verified: Sec 7.5 'Interpreting parameter gradients to understand training and finetuning' proposes to 'project any parameter gradient into the basis defined by the decomposition's subcomponents' and to apply VPD 'to only a weight diff obtained by finetuning'. Also verified: robustness to about 20 adversarial steps but not to 160 or more. These are future work only, and no follow-up appears on Goodfire's research index through 2026-10-15.

Spectral Edge Dynamics (Y. Xu, Mar 2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28964, and Gradient-Direction Sensitivity (Y. Xu, Apr 2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25143. Both take a rolling-window SVD of the parameter-update or gradient trajectory, with a per-mode spectral loss decomposition and grokking timing, across 6 model families from 150K to 124M parameters. This is the nearest ML work that decomposes weight trajectories into time-resolved modes. It is matrix (time × flattened params) rather than CP, has no mechanism library, and treats its directions as diagnostic, not causal.

ExPLAIND (Eichin et al., ICML 2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20076. Model × data × training-step attribution through an AdamW kernel-machine reformulation, with per-scalar-parameter scores summed to layers. Applied to a grokking transformer, where it refines Nanda's three phases. This already gives a mechanism-agnostic 'component × data × time ledger' at layer granularity, so DPD's 'no published method recovers ... which data built it' claim must be narrowed to 'in a learned mechanistic basis'.

POLCA / Hidden Breakthroughs (Kangaslahti, Rosenfeld, Saphra, ICLR 2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15872. Verified: the basis is Hessian eigenvectors built incrementally over checkpoints; per-example loss change is projected per basis vector and clustered with HDBSCAN. The authors write 'Some non-orthogonal basis might represent interpretable concepts more cleanly' and call the ideal basis 'an open question'. DPD Stage 3 is essentially POLCA with an SPD basis, a natural but incremental step.

Don't Forget! Decomposing the Training Dynamics of Memorization (Eichin et al., Sep 2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34933. Decomposes loss trajectories of memorized sequences over training and parameters in Pythia.

Tensor Similarity for Mechanistic Interpretability (Nissen Gonzalez, ..., Riggs Smith, Dooms, May 2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15183. A weight-based, symmetry-invariant metric that tracks grokking and backdoor insertion across checkpoints. It is a competing weight-space developmental instrument for D2.

Transformers learn through gradual rank increase (Abbe et al. 2023), https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.07042. The difference between trained and initial weights progressively increases in rank. This supports DPD's premise and is prior evidence for staged weight-diff growth.

Spectral dynamics of weights (Yunis et al. 2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.11804. Tracks singular values and vectors over training, including grokking. Per-matrix SVD over time is the obvious naive baseline.

Activation-space developmental tools: SAE-Track (https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.17626); Crosscoding Through Time (Bayazit, Mueller, Bosselut, ACL 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.05291); Evolution of Concepts in LM Pre-Training (Ge et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.17196); TCA over continual-learning snapshots, which is tensor decomposition with a snapshot mode but on activations (https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03244).

Competing route to PD identifiability: ASPD, 'Weights Read and Write Features' (Cao, Pruinelli, Thai, Sep 2026), https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37731. It constrains 'otherwise non-unique parameter decompositions' through activation grounding on Qwen-3-8B. DPD should compare against it or position relative to it.
Targeted PD (Vigouroux & Sharkey, ICML 2026 MI workshop), https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13047. Single-checkpoint, with no training-history use.

Susceptibility spectroscopy (Timaeus, Apr 2026), https://timaeus.co/research/2026-04-21-spectroscopy-main. Verified: units are 384 heads, 24 MLPs, embedding and unembedding, on a single Pythia-1.4B checkpoint, and the authors say 'In the future we are likely to use coarser rather than finer subdivisions'. Also Embryology (https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.00331) and Towards Spectroscopy (https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12703).

Model-diffing via PD is only proposed, not done: SPAR 'Towards Exhaustive Model Diffing' (Fall 2026 project description), https://sparai.org/projects/f26/recKEZK7l0JLYEFmL/. The LessWrong post 'Exploration: fine-tuning with parameter decomposition' (https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/ieoWstubDQWLrMnhH/exploration-fine-tuning-with-parameter-decomposition) tunes VPD masks on a single checkpoint and does not decompose diffs.

Verified support claims: Open Problems review (https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16496) Sec 2.1.2d asks for 'a more dynamic, developmental view of how mechanistic structure emerges'. Paulo & Belrose (https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16615) find 30% of features shared across seeds, for SAEs, not PD. Superposition-yields-robust-scaling (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10465) is about model-size scaling only and makes no training-time co-growth claim.

Searches of arXiv (API and site search), OpenAlex, GitHub repositories and the Goodfire research index for CP/PARAFAC/tensor-rank over checkpoints, PD over training, PD of weight diffs, and 'developmental parameter decomposition' returned no paper or repo that combines CP-over-checkpoints with SPD/VPD-style causal decomposition and a mechanism × data × time ledger for transformers. Caveat: the WebSearch budget ran out mid-review and the arXiv API rate-limited, so the LessWrong/AF tag search and the full Semantic Scholar citation graph were not exhaustively checked.
verdicts.fatal_issues:
Nothing I found is fatal to novelty: no published method does the full DPD pipeline. Several issues would sink the paper as written.

(1) The Stage-1 core is not new. CP/low-tensor-rank decomposition of the weight tensor across learning, motivated by Kruskal uniqueness and validated on a GD-trained network, is Pellegrino et al., NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv 2308.11567). The proposal presents 'training history makes weight mechanisms identifiable' as its foundational novelty and does not cite this. Their theory also says GD on low-dimensional tasks yields LOW tensor rank, so the trajectory sits in a fixed low-dimensional subspace. That cuts against recovering many overcomplete mechanisms from the time mode.

(2) The identifiability argument is overstated. Generic CP identifiability up to about d_out·d_in·T/(d_out+d_in+T) assumes generic factor matrices. DPD's own time factors are smooth monotone birth/death splines on log-time. They lie near a few-parameter family (onset, width), so their numerical k-rank is small, far below T. Kruskal needs k_A + k_B + k_C ≥ 2R + 2, so in the superposition regime (R ≫ d), which is exactly where D1 claims the win (ratio ≥ 4), the time mode cannot supply the missing k-rank. Noisy overcomplete CP is also ill-posed: a best rank-R approximation may not exist (de Silva & Lim 2008), and fits show degeneracy. The time mode helps clearly only in the undercomplete or Jennrich regime (R ≤ d, pairwise non-proportional curves).

(3) The pre-registered falsification ablation is mis-specified. A CP decomposition is invariant to permuting the time slices. Shuffling checkpoint order therefore does not remove the identifying information; it only breaks the smoothness and monotonicity prior. If shuffling 'destroys the advantage', that shows prior misspecification, not that development identifies mechanisms. If it doesn't, the pre-registration fails for the wrong reason.

(4) The cheapest competing explanations are missing as baselines:
- per-checkpoint SPD/VPD with Hungarian matching across time;
- final-checkpoint VPD plus projection of ΔW(t) or gradients onto its subcomponents, which is Goodfire's own stated future-work recipe and directly gives growth curves;
- rolling-window update SVD (Spectral Edge);
- for the ledger, POLCA and ExPLAIND.
Without these, D1 to D3 cannot show that DPD, rather than any time-resolved basis, produces the findings.

(5) The motivating gap for D1 is assumed, not shown. There is no published seed-stability or MMCS-collapse number for SPD/VPD at superposition ratio ≥ 4. The 30% figure is for SAEs. I could not verify the quote 'only validated on models where we know what to look for'. SPD already reaches high MMCS on the param-decomp toys, so the headroom may not exist.

(6) H2 framing is wrong. The superposition-scaling paper (2505.10465) concerns model-size scaling and makes no claim that learning co-grows continuously over training time. H2 therefore does not 'adjudicate two live theories of scaling'. It tests the Quantization Model's discreteness prediction against a continuous null.

(7) D2's headline test is weak. Fourier frequencies in a grokked mod-p model are recoverable from final-checkpoint SVD or DFT of W_E. ExPLAIND, Spectral Edge and tensor similarity already re-describe grokking phases from weights and updates.

(8) Calling the ledger 'exact accounting' is an overclaim. The path integral is exact only along the full parameter path. Projecting onto g_c leaves E(t), drift of u_c, and oscillation terms (the LCA failure mode POLCA was built to fix). Adam's coordinate-wise preconditioning also biases ΔW toward axis-aligned changes (arXiv 2604.25143 finds update SVD and gradient SVD differ by 1 to 2 orders of magnitude).

prior_work_found: Stochastic Parameter Decomposition, Bushnaq, Braun & Sharkey 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20790. Table 1 reports final-checkpoint SPD at MMCS 1.000±0.000 on TMS 40-10 (feature/dim ratio 4) and on TMS 5-2, and says the result 'is robust to different training seeds'. It also recovers all 100 features of the ResidualMLP (100 features in 50 neurons). This directly contradicts the premise of D1 that final-checkpoint SPD falls below 0.7 at ratio ≥4 in these toys.

Goodfire VPD, https://www.goodfire.com/research/interpreting-lm-parameters. Section 7.5 lists as future work 'project any parameter gradient into the basis defined by the decomposition's subcomponents' and 'apply VPD to only a weight diff obtained by finetuning'. This confirms the direction is open, and also names windowed weight-diff VPD as the obvious baseline. The page states adversarial robustness holds to about 20 PGD steps and fails at 160 or more.
Targeted Parameter Decomposition (tPD), Vigouroux & Sharkey, June 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13047. Single-checkpoint; no use of checkpoints or time.

Transformers learn through gradual rank increase, Boix-Adsera, Littwin, Abbe, Bengio & Susskind 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.07042. W(t)-W(0) gains rank incrementally. This is the phenomenon Stage 1 relies on, and it gives a trivial incremental-SVD baseline for births.

Exact solutions to the nonlinear dynamics of learning in deep linear networks, Saxe, McClelland & Ganguli 2013, https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6120, and A mathematical theory of semantic development, https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.10531. These show plateau-then-transition learning, mode by mode. This is the regime where the shared-direction CP model is exact. Only the abstracts were verified here.

Tensor Component Analysis, Williams, Kim, Wang, Vyas, Ryu, Shenoy, Schnitzer, Kolda & Ganguli, Neuron 2018 (PMC6907734; DOI 10.1016/j.neuron.2018.05.015). CP/PARAFAC with a learning-time (trial) mode, explicitly applied to datasets from artificial neural networks to recover learning dynamics. That work is in activation space, but it is direct precedent for 'CP with a training-time mode makes components identifiable'.

Toy Models of Superposition, Elhage et al. 2022, https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/toy_model/index.html. Its 'Learning Dynamics' section documents 'energy level jumps' in which features 'jump between different feature dimensionalities and swap places', plus learning as a sequence of 'geometric transformations'. Feature directions therefore move during training in exactly the superposition regime that D1 targets, which violates the shared-u_c,v_c assumption.

Tensor rank and the ill-posedness of the best low-rank approximation problem, de Silva & Lim 2008, https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0607647. Best rank-r CP approximations can fail to exist on sets of positive volume, so near-collinear time factors produce degenerate, diverging component pairs.

Characterizing Learning Curves During Language Model Pre-Training, Chang, Tu & Bergen, https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.15419. It already reports sudden per-token loss changes that are consistent across runs, and that frequent tokens are learned earlier. This pre-empts most of H2 and H3 without any weight decomposition.

POLCA / Hidden Breakthroughs, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15872. Decomposes loss change along bases of the low-rank training subspace and clusters samples by loss-change profile. Stage 3 is POLCA/LCA with a different basis.

LCA, https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.01440. ExPLAIND, https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20076. Quantization Model, https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.13506; its abstract treats frequency-ordered learning as a theoretical premise. Superposition Yields Robust Neural Scaling, https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.10465; its abstract makes claims only about loss versus model width, nothing about training-time co-growth.
Hidden by Optimizer Trajectories, https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25143. AdamW updates rather than gradients change a rolling-SVD diagnostic by 1-2 orders of magnitude; optimizer artifacts are real.

Search caveat: the shared WebSearch budget ran out partway through. I found no published method that fits a shared rank-1 parameter-component library with growth curves across weight checkpoints, or SPD conditioned on checkpoint. Novelty of the exact combination is plausible but not exhaustively confirmed (LessWrong and Alignment Forum, plus 2026 workshop papers, were not fully searched).
verdicts.fatal_issues:
I found no published equivalent of the full method. The proposal still fails as designed: its headline demo targets a baseline failure that the baseline's own paper rules out, its key control is mathematically empty, and its identifiability claim is overstated by orders of magnitude.

1. **The D1 contrast is already refuted by published numbers.** The proposal says DPD wins at ratio ≥4, where final-checkpoint SPD falls below 0.7. SPD's own Table 1 reports MMCS 1.000±0.000 on TMS 40-10 (ratio 4), robust across seeds, and full recovery on the ResidualMLP (2 features per neuron). SPD gets identifiability from input sparsity and causal importance, not from a bare matrix factorisation. So the claim that "a matrix factorization is never unique" attacks a straw version of SPD.
   - In TMS, mechanisms are columns of W (aligned to the input basis). The column norm ||W[:,i](t)|| already gives exact birth times with no decomposition, so birth-time error there is trivially achievable.
   - D1(b) (a trained 2-layer transformer) has no ground-truth mechanism weights, so MMCS is undefined there.

2. **The shuffle ablation cannot test the claimed mechanism.** CP is permutation-equivariant in the time mode. Permuting checkpoints permutes the rows of G and leaves u_c, v_c and the Kruskal k-rank unchanged.
   - If shuffling destroys the advantage, the cause is the order-sensitive monotone-spline/TV prior failing under misspecification, not temporal information.
   - If shuffling does not destroy the advantage, the pre-registered test "fails" even though the method works.
   - More generally, the identifying information sits in the linear span (k-rank) of the growth curves, not in their order or birth times.

3. **The identifiability bound is wildly optimistic.** The quoted generic rank growing with d_out·d_in·T/(d_out+d_in+T) assumes generic time factors. Growth curves are smooth monotone sigmoids. I simulated T=100 log-spaced checkpoints (4 decades), with 50 to 1000 sigmoid growth curves (fixed 0.05-0.3-decade transition widths, random onsets):
   - Raw curves have numerical rank 3-23 regardless of how many there are. Each curve's nearest neighbour has cosine ≈0.9996 or higher.
   - Increments have numerical rank 6-72. The rank is set by log-time span divided by transition width, not by the number of curves.
   - So time can separate roughly 10-50 birth cohorts, not thousands of mechanisms. Kruskal then caps the benefit near R ≲ d + k_G/2. Near-collinear factors make CP ill-posed (de Silva & Lim), producing degenerate, cancelling component pairs.
   - Within a cohort, Stage 2 falls back to ordinary SPD.

4. **Rotation and drift artifacts look exactly like the headline discoveries.** TMS is documented to show features jumping dimensionality, swapping places and undergoing geometric transformations during training.
   - With fixed u_c, v_c, a rotating mechanism is fitted as one component dying plus another being born. That is a spurious "fossil" (H4) and a spurious "birth".
   - H4's validation (ablate at peak vs final) passes such artifacts too, because that direction really did matter at the peak.
   - In real LMs, the embeddings and upstream layers drift, so a fixed residual-stream coordinate does not mean a fixed feature over time.

5. **Optimizer noise mimics births and deaths.** SGD/Adam increments are low-rank updates with step-function time courses, and weight decay makes them shrink. That is exactly the birth/death form. The true CP rank of the trajectory is enormous, and the method has no noise null to set a false-discovery rate for "mechanisms".

6. **D2 does not isolate DPD's added value.** Fourier structure is recoverable from final weights alone: Nanda et al. show the embeddings are sparse in the Fourier basis, so SVD or DFT suffices.
   - The cos/sin pairs share growth curves, so the rotational ambiguity returns within each frequency.
   - The key frequencies likely form concurrently (this needs checking), in which case time does not separate them.
   - Memorisation is high-rank, so it lands in E(t). "Memorization dies" then reduces to a known shrinking weight norm.

7. **D3 has confounds and circularities.**
   - H1: late-learned, low-margin tokens are fragile to any perturbation. A random-window null of about 0 is too weak.
   - H2: the parameterisation (monotone birth spline, sparse death, TV in log-time) builds step-like births in. The per-token test does not need DPD, and Chang et al. already report sudden per-token changes.
   - H3: frequency-ordered learning is already reported (Chang et al.) and is a generic SGD expectation, so it does not discriminate between theories.
   - The superposition-scaling paper makes no training-time claim. "Adjudicates two theories of scaling" is an overclaim.

8. **The Stage 3 ledger is not exact.** It is exact only by definition of the residual. The interpolated path between log-spaced checkpoints is not the training path, and the allocation depends on the path chosen. "Which data built which mechanism" is correlational without data-ablation retraining.
verdicts.fixes:
Re-scope the claim. Drop "training history makes mechanisms identifiable; beats SPD at ratio ≥4". Replace it with two claims:
- (a) Time-cohort separation recovers mechanisms that are co-active in data (and so not separable by causal-importance sparsity) but were built at different times.
- (b) DPD is a developmental instrument: shared component identity across checkpoints, births, deaths, and a ledger. That is the genuinely open gap that Goodfire lists as future work.

**D1 redesign**
1. Before claiming any advantage, show final-checkpoint SPD/VPD failing. Plant pairs of mechanisms whose causal-importance patterns are identical (always co-active on the same inputs) but which differ in function and were trained in separate phases, for example via a curriculum. Also include the reverse control: mechanisms that are separable by data but co-timed, where SPD should match or beat DPD.
2. Use a rotated input basis so mechanisms are not columns, and use planted or teacher weights so ground truth exists. For the transformer toy, use task-purity of causal importance as the metric, or a Tracr-compiled teacher distilled with staged objectives.
3. Replace the shuffle control with temporal-rank controls:
   - project the time mode onto its top-k temporal PCs and show the advantage scales with k;
   - test a rank-1 surrogate trajectory, a(t)W(0) + s(t)(W_T - a_T W(0)), and show the advantage vanishes;
   - vary onset spread divided by transition width, and report the effective temporal rank next to every result.
4. Required baselines:
   - incremental SVD of W(t)-W(0) (Boix-Adsera);
   - SVD or SPD on windowed weight diffs (Goodfire's suggestion);
   - per-checkpoint SPD with Hungarian matching across time;
   - Tucker/HOSVD;
   - per-column norm curves where trivially applicable.
5. Report CP degeneracy diagnostics (core consistency, congruence between components) and a noise null. For the noise null, run DPD on runs that differ only in data order or seed, and on shuffled-label and pure-noise training; count "mechanisms" there to get a false-discovery rate.

**Drift**
- Allow u_c(t) and v_c(t) to drift with a penalty, or fit windowed models.
- Count a death as a transient (H4) only if no born component has matching data and causal-importance profile and functional overlap. That is a successor-matching null.
- Validate transients by data-ablated retraining from the checkpoint before the peak.

**D2**
- Require something final weights cannot give: exact birth order of key frequencies versus excluded-loss inflections; any transient frequencies that are later pruned; agreement with Nanda's restricted and excluded loss timing.
- Baseline against final-checkpoint SPD and DFT/SVD.
- Measure Fourier alignment at the subspace level, given the cos/sin degeneracy.

**D3**
- H1: use a time-matched null (other components born in the same window), norm-matched random rank-1 ablations, and partial correlation controlling for token frequency and final margin.
- H2: fit the competing models with an unregularised (non-monotone, no-TV) variant so the prior cannot decide the answer, and do not claim to test the superposition-scaling paper.
- H3: report it only as a replication.
- Ledger: compute on a dense-checkpoint run (every N steps) so the path matches training, or compare against true per-step LCA on a small model. Validate "which data built c" causally: drop the data cluster, retrain from an earlier checkpoint, and test whether component c fails to form.

**Literature**
Run an explicit novelty check (LessWrong and Alignment Forum, the ICML 2026 MechInterp workshop, Goodfire and Apollo follow-ups) for SPD or VPD across checkpoints. Cite Williams et al. 2018 TCA and Boix-Adsera 2023 as precedent, not as gaps.

redteam.title: Nats of Understanding: turn explanations into executable code, swap them into the model, and measure in nats how much of a network we actually understand

prior_work_found: Gao et al. 2024, Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders, Sec. 4.4 'Explanation reconstruction' (https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04093). This is the closest prior. It asks 'how much performance do we sacrifice if we use only the parts of the model that we can interpret?'. It simulates every SAE latent at GPT-2 small layer 8 (residual stream) from executable N2G n-gram/wildcard explanations, rescales each with E[sa]/E[s^2], decodes, and measures downstream loss against a bigram baseline (Fig. 8). It finds it 'can explain more of GPT-2 small than just explaining bigrams'. It reports one point per SAE, with no bits axis, no richer DSL and no optimization loop.

Paulo & Belrose 2025, Partially Rewriting a Transformer in Natural Language (https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18838). Pythia-160M layer-6 TopK transcoder (32k latents, k=32, with a skip connection), one-sentence explanations, Llama-3-8B simulator with quantile normalization; loss is statistically similar to zero-ablation. Code is on the nl_simulations branch of sae-auto-interp. It does not cite Gao et al. Sec. 4.4.

Bills et al. 2023, Language models can explain neurons in language models (https://openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net/neuron-explainer/paper/index.html). Ablation scoring replaces a single neuron's activations with simulated ones. It also reports that explanation scores fall with layer depth and model size, a precursor to the proposal's 'interpretability scaling law' question (b).

Huang et al. 2023, Rigorously Assessing Natural Language Explanations of Neurons (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10312). GPT-4 explanations have about random-level causal efficacy. The paper explicitly recommends explanations 'grounded in structured formalisms (e.g., programming languages)', so the code-explanation idea has been suggested before but not built at whole-layer scale.
Foote et al. 2023, Neuron to Graph (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.19911). Executable n-gram explanations, validated per neuron against true activations.

Gross et al. 2024, Compact Proofs of Model Performance via Mechanistic Interpretability (https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11779). A frontier of proof length against bound tightness, the toy-model analogue of UF(bits) on Max-of-K transformers.

Gauderis, Dooms, Homer, Ayonrinde, Wiggins 2026, From Mechanistic to Compositional Interpretability (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08934, ICML 2026). A theoretical blueprint that scores explanation quality as faithfulness plus MDL complexity and treats interpretability as constrained optimization. It describes this proposal's objective in theory but appears to run no LM experiments.

Ayonrinde & Jaburi 2025, Evaluating Explanations: An Explanatory Virtues Framework for Mechanistic Interpretability (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01372). A theoretical case for MDL and compact-proof-style evaluation of explanations.

Sharkey, Sparsify: A mechanistic interpretability research agenda (https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/64MizJXzyvrYpeKqm/sparsify-a-mechanistic-interpretability-research-agenda). Frames interpretability as a Pareto frontier of description accuracy against description length, and bets against 'succinct human-understandable explanations' recovering more than 75% of a component's training compute. This is exactly the quantity the harness would measure.
Ayonrinde, Pearce, Sharkey 2024, MDL-SAEs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11179). MDL of codes, not of explanations.

Nguyen 2024, Understanding Transformers via N-gram Statistics (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.12034). Rulesets describe whole-model next-token predictions: about 79% top-1 agreement on TinyStories and 68% on Wikipedia. This is an output-level 'fraction explained by rules'.
Korznikov et al. 2026, Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders (https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14111). Random-baseline SAEs score 0.87 against 0.90 for trained SAEs on interpretability. Verified.

Poché et al. 2026, Limitations of Automated Simulatability: LLM Simulators Can Bypass Explanations (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08585). The setting is ConSim classifier concept explanations, not neuron or latent autointerp, so the proposal's citation of it is analogical.
Lek et al. 2026, Understanding Confabulation and Rethinking Reconstruction in Activation Explanations / Flow-NLA (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33702). Verified.

Anthropic 2026, Natural Language Autoencoders (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2026/nla/). FVE of 0.6-0.8; the visible text reports no spliced downstream-loss measurement and no study of explanation length.

Marin-Llobet & Ferrando 2026, Automated Interpretability and Feature Discovery with Agents (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01555). Agentic hypothesis refinement on Gemma-2 and on weight-sparse MLP neurons, with multi-metric evaluation and no replacement-loss objective.
SAGE, An Agentic Explainer Framework for Interpreting SAE Features (https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20820). Agentic NL explanation refinement scored on generative and predictive accuracy.

Cammarata 2026, Neural Networks Are Already Clean (https://already-clean.goodfire.com/). Audit-percentage evidence (e.g. a Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit of about 90% single-job) and criticism of simulation scoring; no replacement-loss or description-length measurement.

Gao et al. 2025, Weight-sparse transformers have interpretable circuits (https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13653). The '16x smaller circuits' figure does not appear in the abstract; verify its source before using it as a target.

Ameisen et al. 2025, Circuit Tracing (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/methods.html). Replacement and completeness scores measure how much computation runs through features, not through explanations.

Mu & Andreas 2020, Compositional Explanations of Neurons (https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.14032). Executable logical-formula explanations with a formula-length search, scored per neuron by IoU. A precedent for compositional executable explanations with a length budget.
verdicts.fatal_issues:
No substantially equivalent published method was found, but the novelty claim as written is false and must be corrected. The proposal says no paper reports the fraction of a real LM's loss recovered when its units are replaced by human-readable explanations, and that N2G was only scored per neuron. Gao et al. 2024 (arXiv 2406.04093, Sec. 4.4, Fig. 8) did exactly this: they replaced every SAE latent at GPT-2 small layer 8 with N2G-simulated activations (executable n-gram explanations rescaled by E[sa]/E[s^2]), decoded them, measured downstream loss and beat a bigram baseline, framing it as 'how much performance do we sacrifice if we use only the parts of the model that we can interpret?'. The genuinely new parts are narrower: (i) a description-length axis, i.e. the UF(bits) rate-distortion frontier for real-LM units (only toy compact-proofs work and theory papers such as Gauderis et al. 2026 and Sharkey's Sparsify agenda have this); (ii) a compositional DSL beyond n-grams; (iii) loss-weighted agentic optimization with an MDL acceptance rule; (iv) basis and scaling comparisons in nats per bit.

Validity problems that could sink the headline if left unaddressed:
(1) Understanding versus compressibility. With no LLM-free program search over the same primitives as a baseline, a high UF(bits) shows only that unit activations are compressible by surface features, not that the agent 'understands' them. If greedy MDL decision lists or trees, or sparse regression over the DSL feature table, match the agent's frontier, the 'nats of understanding' framing collapses.
(2) The Stage B success bar is too easy. Beating NL plus simulator (about 0% UF) by 3x, or reaching 40% against it, is near-guaranteed by any fitted unigram table or by Gao-style rescaled N2G, because Paulo & Belrose failed largely on calibration and false positives. The pre-registered comparison must be against the strongest automated baseline at equal bits.
(3) Information leakage. Compositional references must read program outputs, never real model activations, or explanations silently import the model's computation. The skip connection of the Paulo & Belrose transcoder must be handled consistently in both the null and the ceiling.
(4) Question (a), superposition versus 'already clean', is overclaimed. Equal-bit basis comparisons are confounded by dictionary reconstruction error, the DSL's bias toward sparse, near-binary units, and the number of units, so a frontier gap measures description compressibility per basis, not superposition directly.
(5) Question (b), the 'first interpretability scaling law', is partly prior: Bills et al. 2023 already showed explainability declining with depth and model size, so the claim must be 'first in nats per bit'.
(6) The budget is implausible. 50M agent tokens over 32k latents is about 1.5k tokens per latent; the 40% target needs a curve over loss-ranked subsets, not the whole dictionary.
(7) Two citations are mis-stated: Poché et al. concerns classifier concept-explanation simulatability, and the '16x smaller circuits' figure is not in the abstract of 2511.13653.
verdicts.fixes:
1. Reposition the contribution. Present it as generalizing Gao et al. 2024 Sec. 4.4 from a single point (N2G, one SAE, one layer) to the first explanation-length versus loss-recovered frontier for real LMs. Explanations become executable, compositional programs, and the MDL acceptance rule makes the frontier an optimizable objective, empirically instantiating Sharkey's Sparsify Pareto frontier and Gauderis et al.'s faithfulness-plus-MDL blueprint. Cite Gao et al., Huang et al. (who called for programming-language explanations), Mu & Andreas, Nguyen 2024 and Gross et al. as direct lineage.

2. Calibrate against the literature (Stage A0). Reproduce Gao et al. Fig. 8 (rescaled N2G on GPT-2 small layer 8, with released OpenAI SAEs) and Paulo & Belrose (Pythia-160M layer 6, using their nl_simulations code) as two calibration points on the same UF axis before claiming any gains.

3. Add the decisive baseline: an LLM-free MDL program search over the identical DSL feature table, such as greedy decision lists or trees, or L0-sparse regression with the same bit accounting. Define a 'semantic surplus' as the agent's frontier minus this frontier. The landmark claim requires a positive surplus at equal bits, together with a blinded human readability and prediction audit showing that people can use the programs. If the surplus is about zero, report that understanding at this level is just feature-compressibility; that is itself a crisp, publishable negative result.

4. Use Korznikov-style random baselines as a falsification control. Build random-direction or frozen-encoder SAEs and transcoders, plus random-rotation and PCA bases, and put them on the same UF(bits) axis. A trained dictionary must dominate random dictionaries on nats per bit; if it does not, the metric has exposed that the features are not real. This settles the dispute that proxy metrics could not.

5. Enforce information flow. Programs may read only the token stream and outputs of other programs, never real activations; enforce this with a dependency-graph check. Report a single-layer swap and a cumulative multi-layer swap separately to expose compounding errors. Use exact swap tests rather than first-order attribution for acceptance decisions.

6. Pre-register Stage B against the strongest equal-bit automated baseline: rescaled N2G, fitted unigram and bigram tables, and the LLM-free MDL search. Do not pre-register against NL plus simulator. Report UF over the loss-ranked top-N latents (N = 256, 1k, 4k) with bootstrap CIs, so the 50M-token budget is realistic.

7. Reframe question (a) as 'which basis gives the best nats per bit frontier at matched reconstruction ceiling', normalizing UF by each basis's own ceiling. Add an explicit argument for why a gap would bear on superposition, for example by showing the neuron-basis programs need disjunctions of unrelated triggers. Credit Bills et al. for the depth and size trend, and make (b) a nats-per-bit scaling law across Pythia sizes and checkpoints.

8. Report robustness to the bit coding with at least three codings (AST gzip, primitive-count prior, and a two-part code with a learned prior over programs), and show that frontier orderings are invariant.

9. Fix the citations. Describe Poché et al. as an analogous shortcut finding in classifier simulatability, and source the weight-sparse '16x' claim from the paper body or blog, or drop it.

No substantially equivalent method was found. The package of a bit-priced, compositional code DSL, whole-layer swap-in, a UF(bits) frontier and a loss-weighted agent loop appears unpublished. As written, however, several demos would not show what they claim.

(1) THE GAP CLAIM IS PARTLY FALSE.
- Gao et al. 2024 §4.4 already swapped executable N2G explanations in for every SAE latent (GPT-2 small, layer 8) and measured downstream loss against a bigram baseline.
- Bills et al. had ablation scoring, and causal scrubbing reports the percentage of loss recovered by hypotheses.
- What is new is the bits axis, the agent optimization and the basis/scaling studies. It is not "the first loss recovered by explanations".

(2) THE HEADLINE CRITERIA ARE CONFOUNDED AND NEARLY GUARANTEED TO PASS.
- Stage B (≥40% versus about 0% for NL+simulator) and Stage A(ii) (3x over N2G and NL+simulator) are measured against weak baselines.
- Paulo & Belrose's null result comes largely from simulator miscalibration: false positives and magnitudes on dense, frequent latents. Any program with fitted lexicons and magnitude maps will beat it, and Gao et al. already showed N2G beats bigrams.
- A pass would show "fitted predictors beat LLM simulators", not that agent-written code adds understanding.
- Stage A(i) is a known fact: MLP0 acts as an extended embedding (Bigram Subnetworks).

(3) THE DECISIVE TRIVIAL BASELINES ARE MISSING.
- (a) Agent-free program search in the SAME DSL at equal bits: greedy MDL, CART, L0-sparse regression over the precomputed token-feature table, and N2G with fitted magnitudes. Without this, the agent loop's contribution is undemonstrated.
- (b) Opaque compression of the layer itself, priced in bits: a quantized, pruned or low-rank MLP or transcoder, or a tiny distilled net over the same features.
- Without (b), UF/bit measures compressibility, not understanding. A program that is mostly lexicons at about 15.6 bits per token is a lookup table in Python syntax, and the human 'readability audit' is the only guard against that.

(4) THE METRIC ITSELF IS NOT VALIDATED.
- Korznikov et al. show that proxy metrics cannot separate trained SAEs from random ones.
- Nothing tests whether UF(bits) separates a trained transcoder from random-baseline dictionaries, neurons from a random rotation, or correct programs from programs assigned to the wrong units.

(5) QUESTIONS (a), (b) AND (d) ARE NOT IDENTIFIED BY THE DESIGN.
- (a) Neuron-versus-transcoder UF per bit is confounded by three things: sparsity (latents that are mostly zero are cheap to predict), unit count (16x more per-program overhead), and the reconstruction ceiling (transcoder error). A polysemantic neuron is just an OR of two cheap programs, so the frontier measures how cheaply each basis can be described in the DSL, not superposition. Cammarata's claim is not stated in loss terms either.
- (b) The bits needed to reach UF=0.5 are a joint property of model, DSL and agent budget. Per-layer CE gaps also shrink with depth and size, which makes matching by relative depth noisy.
- (d) Weight-sparse models (arXiv 2511.13653) are trained on different data and are weaker. Without a dense model matched on data and loss, any explainability gap partly reflects capability.

(6) THE NEGATIVE BRANCH IS UNINFORMATIVE.
- The DSL deliberately has no semantic primitives, so topic and semantic mid-layer features must be enumerated as lexicons, and the frontier is poor by construction.
- A result below 10% therefore cannot separate "not describable at unit level" from "DSL or agent too weak". "Either outcome is a landmark" fails without positive controls.

(7) THE DECOMPILATION CLAIM IS OVERSTATED.
- Only MLP-side units are replaced; attention stays neural.
- The context primitives (previous-k tokens, distance counters, bracket depth) describe input-to-activation behavior and bypass the mechanism. These are behavioral explanations, not a global circuit description.

(8) THERE IS RISK OF ADAPTIVE OVERFITTING.
- Thousands of accept/reject decisions are made on one held-out split.
- Bootstrapping over correlated tokens rather than documents will understate the confidence intervals.
